```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
post <- dirname(normalizePath(knitr::current_input(dir=TRUE),mustWork=TRUE))
d <- read.csv(file.path(post,"data","processed","state_comparison.csv"),stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
top <- read.csv(file.path(post,"results","top_five.csv"),stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
checks <- read.csv(file.path(post,"results","validation.csv"),stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
stopifnot(nrow(d)==50,nrow(top)==5,all(tolower(checks$passed)=="true"),
          file.exists(file.path(post,"figures","rent_burden.html")))
v <- function(abbr,field) d[d$abbr==abbr,field][[1]]
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f",x)
n_increase <- sum(d$change_pp>0)
```

**Which states saw the largest increase in the share of rent-burdened households between 2019 and 2024?** Housing costs matter alongside income: a rent increase need not raise the share of a household’s budget spent on housing if income also rises. The [Census Bureau’s housing report](https://www2.census.gov/library/publications/2025/demo/acs-61.pdf) describes HUD’s common cost-burden benchmark as spending more than 30% of income on housing. Here, I use **at least 30% of household income on rent and utilities**, because the first included Census category is 30.0-34.9%. This is a comparison threshold, not a universal test of affordability. Using all 50 states, I compare how the proportion meeting that threshold changed over five years.

## Measure the pressure on household budgets

I use the Census Bureau's **ACS 1-year estimates**, [table B25070](https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs1/groups/B25070.html), for the same 50 states in both years. Each observation represents a state, not a person. States receive one point each, regardless of their renter populations. DC and Puerto Rico are excluded. The years form a fixed five-year comparison; they are not presented as the latest available data.

Gross rent includes contract rent plus tenant-paid utilities and fuels. The income measure is household income before taxes. I add the four categories from 30% upward and divide by renter households with a computed rent-to-income ratio. The [Census definitions](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf) exclude no-rent households and those reporting zero or negative income from that computable group. Consequently, the percentages do **not** cover every renter household.

This measures the prevalence of a budget burden, not the average rent bill. A higher share means that housing takes at least three dollars of every ten in income for a larger fraction of eligible households.

## Read the states, then narrow the comparison

The Plotly scatterplot places the **2019 share horizontally** and the **2024 share vertically**. Above the dashed no-change line means an increase. The vertical difference between a point and that line is the change in **percentage points**, not percent growth. Both axes keep the same ranges when filtering.

Choose **5 largest estimated increases**, then turn on state labels to identify the leading points without the full cluster. Filter a region to see whether it contains any of those five states. Hover to inspect exact shares, household denominators and the approximate change interval. Selecting a state clears the group filters; **Reset chart** restores all 50.

## Where burdens increased most

The largest point-estimate increases are **Nevada (`r f1(v("NV","change_pp"))` points), Maine (`r f1(v("ME","change_pp"))`), and Florida (`r f1(v("FL","change_pp"))`)**. Arizona and Nebraska complete the top five. Together they span all four Census regions. The increase is therefore not confined to one region in this descriptive ranking.

Nevada rises from **`r f1(v("NV","share_2019"))`% to `r f1(v("NV","share_2024"))`%**. Nebraska rises from **`r f1(v("NE","share_2019"))`% to `r f1(v("NE","share_2024"))`%**, remaining below half despite its large increase. A large estimated increase therefore need not mean the highest current burden.

Reset and inspect Florida. Its **`r f1(v("FL","share_2024"))`%** is the highest 2024 point estimate, although Nevada has the largest estimated increase. California's 2024 share is **`r f1(v("CA","share_2024"))`%**. Its increase is **`r f1(v("CA","change_pp"))` percentage points**, compared with Nevada's **`r f1(v("NV","change_pp"))`**. A ranking based only on the current level would miss where burdens worsened most.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Top five estimated increases

```{r}
tab <- data.frame(State=top$state,`2019 (%)`=f1(top$share_2019),`2024 (%)`=f1(top$share_2024),
                  `Change (pp)`=f1(top$change_pp),
                  `Approx. 90% change interval (pp)`=paste0("[",f1(top$change_low90),", ",f1(top$change_high90),"]"),check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab)
```

:::

## What not to infer

These are survey estimates. Turn on **90% error bars** to see approximate annual uncertainty; hover for the change interval. The [Census approximation formulas](https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2020/acs/acs_general_handbook_2020_ch08.pdf) are documented in the replication guide. These estimates do not establish which state had the largest underlying increase: the intervals are pointwise, not simultaneous ranking intervals.

The surveys also describe different households. Migration, income composition and housing costs could all affect a state's share, but this table cannot separate their contributions. It cannot establish that an individual renter's burden increased, explain a policy's effects, or describe differences between neighborhoods within a state.

## Takeaway

Nevada, Maine and Florida have the largest estimated increases, while Florida has the highest 2024 burden share. The share has a higher point estimate in **`r n_increase` of 50 states**; this does not establish an increase in every one of them. Compare changes as well as levels: a state need not start with the highest burden to experience one of the largest increases.

[Replication instructions and saved-source provenance](README.md) accompany the data and code. Rendering reuses local results without downloading again.
